title: Convergent evolutionary adaptations in wing morphology enable flight among miniaturized bark beetles
content:
Abstract
Miniaturization repeatedly opens new ecological opportunities, but in winged insects it also creates a physical bottleneck: under isometric scaling, aerodynamic force declines faster with size than body weight, producing a weight-support shortfall in tiny flyers. Here, we show that minute bark beetles repeatedly compensate for this ‘force gap’ through convergent optimization of wing design. The smallest taxa cluster within a narrow region of wing morphospace, with independent tests supporting convergence among distantly related miniaturized lineages. This convergence reflects a predictable link between form and function: in a quasi-steady aerodynamic framework, force scales linearly with the second moment of wing area, S2. Across 39 species, S2 showed negative allometry, with an exponent close to that required to maintain weight support through changes in S2 alone. Decomposition of S2 revealed a size-dependent shift in compensatory strategy: larger species rely mainly on wingspan elongation, whereas minute taxa increase normalized S2 by redistributing wing area distally, producing spatulate wings with greater aerodynamic leverage. Ornstein–Uhlenbeck modelling indicates that shape optimization evolves more slowly than wingspan elongation, suggesting stronger phylogenetic constraint. Thus, miniaturization does not merely favour aerodynamic optimization; by intensifying physical constraints, it channels evolution towards a narrow set of mechanically viable wing designs.
